props.title: Slugs
props.initialSlug: Killer slugs terrorize a small town with deadly slime

sections.content: Slugs (1988) stands as a gloriously grotesque entry in the nature-gone-wild horror subgenre that flourished in the 1970s and 80s. Spanish director Juan Piquer Simón, who also helmed the wonderfully deranged Pieces (1982), crafts a gleefully disgusting creature feature that follows the tradition of Night of the Creeps (1986) and The Deadly Spawn (1983). Based on Shaun Hutson's novel, the film amplifies the gross-out elements while maintaining that distinct Euro-horror aesthetic that characterized many Spanish-American co-productions of the era.

sections.content: The killer slug subgenre, while niche, connects to the broader eco-horror movement that gave us classics like Frogs (1972) and Kingdom of the Spiders (1977). These films channeled growing environmental anxieties through the lens of creature features. Slugs distinguishes itself through its unflinching gore and practical effects work that rivals contemporary Italian horror productions like Demons (1985).

The film's greatest strength lies in its commitment to practical effects and gore setpieces. Unlike many of its contemporaries that relied on rubber puppets filmed in shadow, Slugs presents its monsters in full, well-lit glory. The death scenes are inventive and shocking, particularly the infamous restaurant sequence that rivals similar moments in Street Trash (1987) and The Stuff (1985). sections.content: Slugs represents an important entry in Spanish genre cinema of the 1980s, alongside films like Pieces (1982) and Pod People (1983). These productions often combined American horror conventions with distinctly European sensibilities, resulting in unique hybrid films that pushed boundaries in terms of gore and shock value while maintaining artistic flourishes characteristic of Spanish cinema.
